content: Burnout in men is a state of emotional, physical, and mental exhaustion caused by prolonged and excessive stress, especially related to work or caregiving roles. It is characterized by three major components: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization (cynicism or detachment), and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. This syndrome is recognized globally by the World Health Organization as an occupational phenomenon, but it can affect men in various life domains including family, social, and health contexts. Physiologically, burnout involves dysregulation of the stress response systems, including the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and autonomic nervous system, which can contribute to poor health outcomes like cardiovascular disease. Men may experience burnout symptoms differently or underreport them due to social norms and stigma around expressing vulnerability, which affects recognition and support. Evidence-based approaches to prevention and treatment include stress management techniques, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), workplace interventions, and lifestyle modifications such as exercise and adequate sleep. Practical relevance includes promoting resilience and early identification to prevent long-term impairment. Limitations in current knowledge include the variability in diagnostic criteria and underrepresentation of men in research. Safety considerations emphasize avoiding burnout exacerbation through adequate rest, avoiding substance misuse, and seeking professional help. Major synonyms and related terms include occupational stress, work fatigue, emotional exhaustion syndrome, and chronic stress. This module provides a comprehensive overview for consumers and providers to recognize, prevent, and manage burnout in men safely and effectively.

content: Burnout is a multidimensional syndrome defined by emotional exhaustion (feeling drained and depleted), depersonalization or cynicism (developing a detached or negative attitude towards work or roles), and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment (feeling ineffective or unproductive). Although extensively studied as an occupational phenomenon, burnout also affects men in family caregiving and community roles. The World Health Organization classifies burnout as an occupational phenomenon in the ICD-11 (code QD85), not a medical condition, emphasizing its link to chronic workplace stress unresponsive to coping efforts. Synonyms include occupational stress syndrome, work fatigue, and emotional exhaustion syndrome.

content: Several work-related factors contribute to burnout in men including high job demands, low job control, inadequate social support, and job insecurity. Lifestyle factors such as poor sleep, sedentary behavior, and substance use can worsen burnout severity. Understanding these contributors aids in targeted prevention.
